propertyBank.definition: "Total Angular Momentum" combines both the spin and orbital angular momentum of all particles and fields.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: "Total Angular Momentum" combines both the spin and orbital angular momentum of all particles and fields. In atomic and nuclear physics, orbital angular momentum is usually denoted by $l$ or $L$ instead of $\Lambda$. The magnitude of $J$ is quantized so that $J^2 = \hbar^2 j(j + 1)$, where $j$ is the total angular momentum quantum number.

propertyBank.definition: The "Total Angular Quantum Number" describes the magnitude of total angular momentum $J$, where $j$ refers to a specific particle and $J$ is used for the whole system.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: The "Total Angular Quantum Number" describes the magnitude of total angular momentum $J$, where $j$ refers to a specific particle and $J$ is used for the whole system.

propertyBank.definition: The "Total Atomic Stopping Power" for an ionizing particle passing through an element, is the particle's energy loss per atom within a unit area normal to the particle's path; equal to the linear energy transfer (energy loss per unit path l
propertyBank.fullDefinition: The "Total Atomic Stopping Power" for an ionizing particle passing through an element, is the particle's energy loss per atom within a unit area normal to the particle's path; equal to the linear energy transfer (energy loss per unit path length) divided by the number of atoms per unit volume.

propertyBank.definition: "Total Cross-section" is related to the absorbance of the light intensity through Beer-Lambert's law.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: "Total Cross-section" is related to the absorbance of the light intensity through Beer-Lambert's law. It is the sum of all cross-sections corresponding to the various reactions or processes between an incident particle of specified type and energy and a target particle.

propertyBank.definition: "Total Current" is the sum of the electric current that is flowing through a surface and the displacement current.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: "Total Current" is the sum of the electric current that is flowing through a surface and the displacement current.

propertyBank.definition: "Total Current Density" is the sum of the electric current density and the displacement current density.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: "Total Current Density" is the sum of the electric current density and the displacement current density.

propertyBank.definition: "Total Ionization" by a particle, total mean charge, divided by the elementary charge, $e$, of all positive ions produced by an ionizing charged particle along its entire path and along the paths of any secondary charged particles.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: "Total Ionization" by a particle, total mean charge, divided by the elementary charge, $e$, of all positive ions produced by an ionizing charged particle along its entire path and along the paths of any secondary charged particles.

propertyBank.definition: The "Total Linear Stopping Power" is defined as the average energy loss of the particle per unit path length.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: The "Total Linear Stopping Power" is defined as the average energy loss of the particle per unit path length.

propertyBank.definition: If a substance is compared in gaseous and solid form, then the linear stopping powers of the two states are very different just because of the different density.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: If a substance is compared in gaseous and solid form, then the linear stopping powers of the two states are very different just because of the different density. One therefore often divides S(E) by the density of the material to obtain the "Mass Stopping Power". The mass stopping power then depends only very little on the density of the material.

propertyBank.definition: The total pressure is the sum of the dynamic and static pressures, that is $P_0 = P + q$.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: The total pressure is the sum of the dynamic and static pressures, that is $P_0 = P + q$.

propertyBank.definition: "Touch Thresholds" is an umbrella term for the thresholds of sensitivity of the skin to touch, vibration and other mechanical stimuli.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: "Touch Thresholds" is an umbrella term for the thresholds of sensitivity of the skin to touch, vibration and other mechanical stimuli. It has no single dimension: a concrete touch threshold specializes into a force for light-touch detection (e.g. von Frey monofilaments, in millinewtons), a length for vibration-detection amplitude or two-point separation, or a pressure, depending on the stimulus and method.

propertyBank.definition: Transmittance is the fraction of incident light (electromagnetic radiation) at a specified wavelength that passes through a sample.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: Transmittance is the fraction of incident light (electromagnetic radiation) at a specified wavelength that passes through a sample.

propertyBank.definition: Transmittance is the fraction of incident light (electromagnetic radiation) at a specified wavelength that passes through a sample.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: Transmittance is the fraction of incident light (electromagnetic radiation) at a specified wavelength that passes through a sample.

propertyBank.definition: Turbidity is the cloudiness or haziness of a fluid, or of air, caused by individual particles (suspended solids) that are generally invisible to the naked eye, similar to smoke in air.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: Turbidity is the cloudiness or haziness of a fluid, or of air, caused by individual particles (suspended solids) that are generally invisible to the naked eye, similar to smoke in air. Turbidity in open water is often caused by phytoplankton and the measurement of turbidity is a key test of water quality. The higher the turbidity, the higher the risk of the drinkers developing gastrointestinal diseases, especially for immune-compromised people, because contaminants like virus or bacteria can become attached to the suspended solid. The suspended solids interfere with water disinfection with chlorine because the particles act as shields for the virus and bacteria. Similarly suspended solids can protect bacteria from UV sterilisation of water. Fluids can contain suspended solid matter consisting of particles of many different sizes. While some suspended material will be large enough and heavy enough to settle rapidly to the bottom container if a liquid sample is left to stand (the settleable solids), very small particles will settle only very slowly or not at all if the sample is regularly agitated or the particles are colloidal. These small solid particles cause the liquid to appear turbid.

propertyBank.definition: "Turns" is the number of turns in a winding.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: "Turns" is the number of turns in a winding.

propertyBank.fullDefinition: Placeholder value used for reference from units where it is not clear what a given unit is a measure of.

propertyBank.fullDefinition: "Upper Critical Magnetic Flux Density" for type II superconductors, is the threshold magnetic flux density for disappearance of bulk superconductivity.

propertyBank.fullDefinition: The moisture transmission rate of a material is referred to as its "permeability".

propertyBank.definition: A material's "permeance", is dependent on thickness much like the R-value in heat transmission.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: A material's "permeance", is dependent on thickness much like the R-value in heat transmission. Dividing the permeability of a material by its thickness gives the material's permeance. Permeance is the number that should be used to compare various products in regard to moisture transmission resistance.

propertyBank.definition: A pressure that is the one exerted by a substance vapour in thermodynamic equilibrium with either its solid or liquid phase at a given temperature in a closed system.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: A pressure that is the one exerted by a substance vapour in thermodynamic equilibrium with either its solid or liquid phase at a given temperature in a closed system.

Dividing the permeability of a material by its thickness gives the material's permeance. Permeance is the number that should be used to compare various products in regard to moisture transmission resistance.

propertyBank.fullDefinition: A pressure that is the one exerted by a substance vapour in thermodynamic equilibrium with either its solid or liquid phase at a given temperature in a closed system.

propertyBank.definition: In kinematics, velocity is the speed of an object and a specification of its direction of motion.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: In kinematics, velocity is the speed of an object and a specification of its direction of motion. Speed describes only how fast an object is moving, whereas velocity gives both how fast and in what direction the object is moving.

propertyBank.definition: Ventilation Rate is often expressed by the volumetric flowrate of outdoor air introduced to a building.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: Ventilation Rate is often expressed by the volumetric flowrate of outdoor air introduced to a building. However, ASHRAE now recommends ventilation rates dependent upon floor area.

propertyBank.definition: The rate at which a body moves upwards at an angle of 90 degrees to the ground.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: The rate at which a body moves upwards at an angle of 90 degrees to the ground. It is the component of a projectile's velocity which is concerned with lifting the projectile.

propertyBank.definition: "Density of States" is the number of vibrational modes in an infinitesimal interval of angular frequency divided by the range of that interval and by volume.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: "Density of States" is the number of vibrational modes in an infinitesimal interval of angular frequency divided by the range of that interval and by volume.

propertyBank.definition: Frame rate (also known as frame frequency) is the frequency (rate) at which an imaging device produces unique consecutive images called frames.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: Frame rate (also known as frame frequency) is the frequency (rate) at which an imaging device produces unique consecutive images called frames. The term applies equally well to computer graphics, video cameras, film cameras, and motion capture systems. Frame rate is most often expressed in frames per second (FPS) and is also expressed in progressive scan monitors as hertz (Hz).

propertyBank.definition: Viscosity is a measure of the resistance of a fluid which is being deformed by either shear stress or extensional stress.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: Viscosity is a measure of the resistance of a fluid which is being deformed by either shear stress or extensional stress. In general terms it is the resistance of a liquid to flow, or its "thickness". Viscosity describes a fluid's internal resistance to flow and may be thought of as a measure of fluid friction. [Wikipedia]. In general conversation or in non-scientific contexts, if someone refers to the viscosity of a fluid, they're likely talking about its dynamic (or absolute) viscosity. However, in engineering or scientific contexts, it's essential to clarify which type of viscosity is being discussed, as the interpretation and use of the data may differ depending on whether one is talking about dynamic or kinematic viscosity.

propertyBank.definition: "Visible Radiant Energy", also known as luminous energy, is the energy of electromagnetic waves.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: "Visible Radiant Energy", also known as luminous energy, is the energy of electromagnetic waves. It is energy of the particles that are emitted, transferred, or received as radiation.

propertyBank.definition: "Vision Thresholds" is the thresholds of sensitivity of the eye.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: "Vision Thresholds" is the thresholds of sensitivity of the eye.

propertyBank.definition: $\textit{Voltage}$, also referred to as $\textit{Electric Tension}$, is the difference between electrical potentials of two points.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: $\textit{Voltage}$, also referred to as $\textit{Electric Tension}$, is the difference between electrical potentials of two points. For an electric field within a medium, $U_{ab} = - \int_{r_a}^{r_b} E . {dr}$, where $E$ is electric field strength. For an irrotational electric field, the voltage is independent of the path between the two points $a$ and $b$.

propertyBank.definition: Voltage imbalance is the percentage deviation of individual phase voltages from the average voltage across phases in a polyphase electrical system.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: Voltage imbalance is the percentage deviation of individual phase voltages from the average voltage across phases in a polyphase electrical system.

propertyBank.definition: "Voltage Phasor" is a representation of voltage as a sinusoidal integral quantity using a complex quantity whose argument is equal to the initial phase and whose modulus is equal to the root-mean-square value.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: "Voltage Phasor" is a representation of voltage as a sinusoidal integral quantity using a complex quantity whose argument is equal to the initial phase and whose modulus is equal to the root-mean-square value. A phasor is a constant complex number, usually expressed in exponential form, representing the complex amplitude (magnitude and phase) of a sinusoidal function of time. Phasors are used by electrical engineers to simplify computations involving sinusoids, where they can often reduce a differential equation problem to an algebraic one.

propertyBank.definition: The volume of a solid object is the three-dimensional concept of how much space it occupies, often quantified numerically.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: The volume of a solid object is the three-dimensional concept of how much space it occupies, often quantified numerically. One-dimensional figures (such as lines) and two-dimensional shapes (such as squares) are assigned zero volume in the three-dimensional space.

propertyBank.definition: Volumetric Flow Rate, (also known as volume flow rate, rate of fluid flow or volume velocity) is the volume of fluid which passes through a given surface per unit time.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: Volumetric Flow Rate, (also known as volume flow rate, rate of fluid flow or volume velocity) is the volume of fluid which passes through a given surface per unit time.

propertyBank.definition: Volume flow ratio is commonly used in fluid dynamics and engineering, referring to the ratio of the flow rates of two or more fluid streams within a system.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: Volume flow ratio is commonly used in fluid dynamics and engineering, referring to the ratio of the flow rates of two or more fluid streams within a system. In HVAC systems, the flow ratio could compare the amount of fresh air introduced to the amount of recirculated air.

propertyBank.definition: "Volume Fraction" is the volume of a constituent divided by the volume of all constituents of the mixture prior to mixing.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: "Volume Fraction" is the volume of a constituent divided by the volume of all constituents of the mixture prior to mixing. Volume fraction is also called volume concentration in ideal solutions where the volumes of the constituents are additive (the volume of the solution is equal to the sum of the volumes of its ingredients).

propertyBank.fullDefinition: Volume, or volumetric, Strain, or dilatation (the relative variation of the volume) is the trace of the tensor $\vartheta$.

propertyBank.definition: When the temperature of a substance changes, the energy that is stored in the intermolecular bonds between atoms changes.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: When the temperature of a substance changes, the energy that is stored in the intermolecular bonds between atoms changes. When the stored energy increases, so does the length of the molecular bonds. As a result, solids typically expand in response to heating and contract on cooling; this dimensional response to temperature change is expressed by its coefficient of thermal expansion. Different coefficients of thermal expansion can be defined for a substance depending on whether the expansion is measured by: * linear thermal expansion * area thermal expansion * volumetric thermal expansion These characteristics are closely related. The volumetric thermal expansion coefficient can be defined for both liquids and solids. The linear thermal expansion can only be defined for solids, and is common in engineering applications. Some substances expand when cooled, such as freezing water, so they have negative thermal expansion coefficients. [Wikipedia]

propertyBank.fullDefinition: In fluid dynamics, the volumetric flux is the rate of volume flow across a unit area (m3·s−1·m−2).[Wikipedia]

propertyBank.definition: $\textit{Volumetric Heat Capacity (VHC)}$, also termed $\textit{volume-specific heat capacity}$, describes the ability of a given volume of a substance to store internal energy while undergoing a given temperature change, but without underg
propertyBank.fullDefinition: $\textit{Volumetric Heat Capacity (VHC)}$, also termed $\textit{volume-specific heat capacity}$, describes the ability of a given volume of a substance to store internal energy while undergoing a given temperature change, but without undergoing a phase transition. It is different from specific heat capacity in that the VHC is a $\textit{per unit volume}$ measure of the relationship between thermal energy and temperature of a material, while the specific heat is a $\textit{per unit mass}$ measure (or occasionally per molar quantity of the material).

propertyBank.definition: $\textit{Volumic Electromagnetic Energy}$, also known as the $\textit{Electromagnetic Energy Density}$, is the energy associated with an electromagnetic field, per unit volume of the field.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: $\textit{Volumic Electromagnetic Energy}$, also known as the $\textit{Electromagnetic Energy Density}$, is the energy associated with an electromagnetic field, per unit volume of the field.

propertyBank.definition: In the simplest sense, vorticity is the tendency for elements of a fluid to "spin." More formally, vorticity can be related to the amount of "circulation" or "rotation" (or more strictly, the local angular rate of rotation) in a fluid.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: In the simplest sense, vorticity is the tendency for elements of a fluid to "spin." More formally, vorticity can be related to the amount of "circulation" or "rotation" (or more strictly, the local angular rate of rotation) in a fluid. The average vorticity in a small region of fluid flow is equal to the circulation C around the boundary of the small region, divided by the area A of the small region. Mathematically, vorticity is a vector field and is defined as the curl of the velocity field.

propertyBank.definition: "Warm Receptor Threshold" is the threshold of warm-sensitive free nerve-ending.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: "Warm Receptor Threshold" is the threshold of warm-sensitive free nerve-ending.

propertyBank.definition: The "Warping Constant" is a measure for the warping constant or warping resistance of a cross section under torsional loading.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: The "Warping Constant" is a measure for the warping constant or warping resistance of a cross section under torsional loading. It is usually measured in m⁶.

propertyBank.definition: The warping moment measure is a measure for the warping moment, which occurs in warping torsional analysis.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: The warping moment measure is a measure for the warping moment, which occurs in warping torsional analysis. It is usually measured in kNm².

propertyBank.definition: No pump can convert all of its mechanical power into water power.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: No pump can convert all of its mechanical power into water power. Mechanical power is lost in the pumping process due to friction losses and other physical losses. It is because of these losses that the horsepower going into the pump has to be greater than the water horsepower leaving the pump. The efficiency of any given pump is defined as the ratio of the water horsepower out of the pump compared to the mechanical horsepower into the pump.

propertyBank.definition: An amount of substance per unit volume that is the concentration of a saturated solution expressed as the ratio of the solute concentration over the volume of water.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: An amount of substance per unit volume that is the concentration of a saturated solution expressed as the ratio of the solute concentration over the volume of water. A substance's solubility fundamentally depends on several physical and chemical properties of the solution as well as the environment it is in.

propertyBank.definition: The Water vapour diffusion coefficient describes how easy vapour diffusion happens in a given material.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: The Water vapour diffusion coefficient describes how easy vapour diffusion happens in a given material.

propertyBank.definition: The Water vapour diffusion coefficient describes how easy vapour diffusion happens in a given material.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: The Water vapour diffusion coefficient describes how easy vapour diffusion happens in a given material.

propertyBank.definition: For a monochromatic wave, "wavelength" is the distance between two successive points in a direction perpendicular to the wavefront where at a given instant the phase differs by $2\pi$.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: For a monochromatic wave, "wavelength" is the distance between two successive points in a direction perpendicular to the wavefront where at a given instant the phase differs by $2\pi$. The wavelength of a sinusoidal wave is the spatial period of the wave—the distance over which the wave's shape repeats. The SI unit of wavelength is the meter.

propertyBank.definition: "Wavenumber" is the spatial frequency of a wave - the number of waves that exist over a specified distance.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: "Wavenumber" is the spatial frequency of a wave - the number of waves that exist over a specified distance. More formally, it is the reciprocal of the wavelength. It is also the magnitude of the wave vector. Light passing through different media keeps its frequency, but not its wavelength or wavenumber. The unit for wavenumber commonly used in spectroscopy is centimetre to power minus one, PER-CM, rather than metre to power minus one, PER-M.

propertyBank.definition: The force with which a body is attracted toward an astronomical body.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: The force with which a body is attracted toward an astronomical body. Or, the product of the mass of a body and the acceleration acting on a body. In a dynamic situation, the weight can be a multiple of that under resting conditions. Weight also varies on other planets in accordance with their gravity.

propertyBank.definition: the temperature of a parcel of air cooled to saturation (100% relative humidity) by the evaporation of water into it, with the latent heat supplied by the parcel.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: the temperature of a parcel of air cooled to saturation (100% relative humidity) by the evaporation of water into it, with the latent heat supplied by the parcel.

propertyBank.definition: "Width" is the middle of three dimensions: length, width, thickness.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: "Width" is the middle of three dimensions: length, width, thickness.

propertyBank.definition: A force is said to do Work when it acts on a body so that there is a displacement of the point of application, however small, in the direction of the force.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: A force is said to do Work when it acts on a body so that there is a displacement of the point of application, however small, in the direction of the force. The concepts of work and energy are closely tied to the concept of force because an applied force can do work on an object and cause a change in energy. Energy is defined as the ability to do work. Work is done on an object when an applied force moves it through a distance. Kinetic energy is the energy of an object in motion. The net work is equal to the change in kinetic energy.

propertyBank.definition: "Work Function" is the energy difference between an electron at rest at infinity and an electron at a certain energy level.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: "Work Function" is the energy difference between an electron at rest at infinity and an electron at a certain energy level. The minimum energy (usually measured in electronvolts) needed to remove an electron from a solid to a point immediately outside the solid surface (or energy needed to move an electron from the Fermi level into vacuum).

propertyBank.definition: Zenith angle is the angle measured from the zenith (the point directly overhead) downward to a celestial object or direction of interest.
propertyBank.fullDefinition: Zenith angle is the angle measured from the zenith (the point directly overhead) downward to a celestial object or direction of interest. It is the complement of the elevation (altitude) angle.

the property of radiation that enables it to produce photochemical effects
(physics) the property of being isotropic; having the same value when measured in different directions
the property of being anisotropic; having a different value when measured in different directions
